name: Ginger
summary: A spicy root best known for settling the stomach. In small trials it eased nausea in early pregnancy and period pain, and nudged blood sugar and blood pressure down a little.
inIt: Gingerols, mainly 6-gingerol, are the main pungent compounds of the fresh root. A review links them to ginger's reputed effects on nausea, arthritis and pain; which compounds cause any effect in people is not known.
Shogaols form when gingerols lose water during drying and heating. They give dried ginger its sharper taste. In water the change goes both ways and settles at a balance.

Paradols: in mice, 6-paradol is the main breakdown product of 6-shogaol. In cell studies, 6-paradol and 6-shogaol made fat and muscle cells take up more glucose; whether this happens in people is not known.
Zingerone is one of the five main compounds measured in fresh, dried, stir-fried and charred ginger, next to 6-, 8- and 10-gingerol and 6-shogaol.
Volatile oils: one analysis of dried Australian ginger found 100 volatile compounds, including 54 terpenoid compounds and 35 related to gingerols, some never reported in ginger before.

The food table (CoFID) lists energy, protein, fat, carbohydrate, fibre, minerals and some vitamins for fresh and ground ginger. It measures none of the compounds above, so the nutrient numbers for ginger say nothing about what ginger is studied for.

history.use: Fresh ginger, called "the holy medicine of vomiting", to stop vomiting, including in pregnancy
history.finding: Nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
history.note: In small trials, mostly of ground ginger in capsules, ginger eased nausea in early pregnancy compared with a dummy pill, but did not clearly reduce vomiting. For sickness after surgery or during chemotherapy, results were mixed.

history.use: Ginger for arthritis, rheumatism and aching muscles
history.note: Trials of plain ground ginger for knee osteoarthritis are few and small: one blinded trial found no benefit over a dummy pill, and an open-label one found it added a little to a painkiller. The clearer benefits reported in reviews come from concentrated extracts, a different product.

history.note: In short trials, ginger supplements went with blood pressure a few mmHg lower, mostly in people with raised blood pressure or obesity. Certainty is low, and in type 2 diabetes the fall was small.

history.note: No trial in people was found for this page. The Persian texts reasoned from ginger's "hot and dry" nature, an idea modern studies don't measure.

history.use: Ginger in remedies for the mouth, teeth, eyes and voice, and for people with leprosy
history.note: Ginger was found in the hardened plaque on the teeth of 7 people buried at the leprosy hospital of St Leonard in Peterborough, 6 of them with signs of leprosy in their bones. That shows it was eaten or held in the mouth, not whether it helped, and no study in people of ginger for leprosy was found for this page.

sources.title: First archaeological evidence for ginger consumption as a potential medicinal ingredient in a late medieval leprosarium at St Leonard, Peterborough, England.

processing: Fresh or dried: drying and heating turn gingerols into shogaols. In one laboratory study moist heat made more shogaol than dry heat (up to 2,991 mg of 6-shogaol per kg of ginger after 360 minutes at 120 °C), and dry heat on ground ginger made more than dry heat on fresh slices.
In another analysis, dried ginger had 5.2 times the phenolic content of fresh ginger. Stir-frying and charring lowered gingerols and raised shogaols.

How ginger is dried matters too: in a 2026 study, drying at 120 °C then 80 °C gave more gingerols than drying at 80 °C alone (11.87 against 7.12 mg per g), but kept less volatile oil (1.29% against 3.46%).

Capsules of ground ginger are the dried food. Concentrated extracts are different products: trials have used a carbon dioxide (CO₂) extract, capsules of pure 6-gingerol, extracts standardised to 5% gingerols, and an extract of ginger with galangal (EV.EXT 77). Results from extracts can't be taken as results for eating ginger.

Ginger tea and drinks: the amount of gingerols in ginger teas and drinks varied widely in a 2007 US analysis, and so did the amount in nine ginger supplements. None of the trials on this page tested ginger ale.
Ginger biscuits and crystallised ginger: one pregnancy trial used ginger biscuits (2,500 mg of ginger a day). No trial found for this page tested crystallised (candied) ginger.
whatStudiesDid: Most trials gave ground (dried) ginger root in capsules, for days or weeks. In early pregnancy, most trials gave 1,000 to 1,950 mg a day of ginger powder in capsules for about 4 days; others used ginger biscuits (2,500 mg a day), syrup, an extract or an essence, and several compared ginger with vitamin B6 rather than a dummy pill. Before surgery, trials gave a fixed amount of at least 1 g. During chemotherapy, ginger was added to the usual anti-sickness medicines: often powdered root at 0.5 to 1.5 g a day for 3 to 5 days, but also concentrated extracts, 6-gingerol capsules and ginger tea. For period pain, women (mostly students in Iran) had 750 to 2,000 mg of crude dry ginger powder a day, usually on the first 3 days of one period. In type 2 diabetes, trials gave 1,200 to 3,000 mg a day for 8 to 12 weeks; 10 of 13 were in Iran. These describe the studies; they are not amounts for anyone to follow.

findings.outcome: Nausea and vomiting in early pregnancy
findings.population: Pregnant women with nausea and vomiting, mostly in early pregnancy; most trials used ground ginger in capsules for about 4 days
whyThisGrade: The review's own authors rated the evidence low quality: few, small trials with outcomes measured in different ways
Nausea improved, but the number of vomiting episodes was not clearly lower
Several trials compared ginger with vitamin B6 rather than a dummy pill, and a few used syrup, extract or essence instead of ground ginger
The Cochrane review of all treatments found the evidence for ginger limited and not consistent
Safety comes mostly from one cohort in which women reported ginger use themselves
findings.summary: In a 2014 review of 12 randomised trials with 1,278 pregnant women, ginger improved nausea compared with a dummy pill (mean difference in nausea scores 1.20, 95% confidence interval 0.56 to 1.84), but the number of vomiting episodes was not clearly lower (0.72, −0.03 to 1.46). Most trials gave ginger powder in capsules, 1,000 to 1,950 mg a day, usually for 4 days; the authors rated the evidence low quality. A 2022 review of 13 trials (1,174 women) found the same pattern against a dummy pill, and no clear difference between ginger and vitamin B6. The Cochrane review of all treatments for nausea in early pregnancy (41 trials, 5,449 women, 2015) said ginger products may help, but the evidence was limited and not consistent, and found no high-quality evidence for any treatment. On safety, miscarriage was not significantly more common with ginger than with a dummy pill in the 2014 review (risk ratio 3.14, 0.65 to 15.11, a very wide interval), and heartburn and drowsiness were not more common. In a Norwegian cohort of 68,522 pregnant women, the 1,020 (1.5%) who used ginger had no higher risk of birth defects, stillbirth, preterm birth, low birth weight or a low Apgar score.
findings.bottomLine: In small trials, mostly of ground ginger in capsules for a few days, ginger eased nausea in early pregnancy compared with a dummy pill, but did not clearly reduce vomiting. The evidence is low quality. A large Norwegian cohort found no higher risk of birth defects or other birth problems in women who used ginger.
findings.label: Nausea in early pregnancy
findings.line: Eased nausea in small trials, mostly capsules; vomiting not clearly reduced

findings.population: Adults having surgery, given ginger by mouth before the operation (mostly ground ginger in capsules)
whyThisGrade: Reviews disagree: some found fewer people sick, others only milder nausea with no clear difference in vomiting or the need for anti-sickness medicine
Many small trials with different amounts, timing and kinds of surgery
A network review found the clearest result for ginger oil, a different product from eating ginger
findings.summary: A 2006 review of 5 trials (363 patients) found fewer people with nausea or vomiting in the 24 hours after surgery when they had a fixed amount of at least 1 g of ginger beforehand (relative risk 0.69, 95% confidence interval 0.54 to 0.89) and fewer with vomiting (0.61, 0.45 to 0.84); abdominal discomfort was the only side effect reported. Later reviews were less clear. In 10 trials (918 patients, 2018), nausea and vomiting were milder (standardised mean difference −0.247, −0.455 to −0.040), but fewer people being sick or needing anti-sickness medicine could have been chance. In 14 trials (1,417 people, 2021), nausea was milder (mean difference −0.71, −1.37 to −0.06) and fewer people needed rescue anti-sickness medicine (relative risk 0.71, 0.62 to 0.82). In another review of 14 trials (1,506 patients, 2022), nausea scores were lower 2, 6 and 12 hours after surgery, but vomiting, nausea-and-vomiting and the use of anti-sickness medicine did not differ except in the recovery room.
findings.bottomLine: Ginger before surgery made nausea afterwards somewhat milder in several reviews, but whether fewer people were sick or needed anti-sickness medicine differed between reviews. The trials were small and varied.
findings.label: Nausea after surgery
findings.line: Somewhat milder nausea in reviews; whether fewer people were sick differed

findings.population: Adults having chemotherapy, with ginger added to their usual anti-sickness medicines
whyThisGrade: Overall, nausea and vomiting were not clearly different; the benefit for early (acute) vomiting comes from subgroups of a few trials
The reviews mix ground ginger root with concentrated extracts (a CO₂ extract, 6-gingerol capsules, extracts with 5% gingerols) and ginger tea
Trials differed in chemotherapy, amounts and timing
findings.summary: A 2019 review of 18 articles found that, with 1 g a day or less for more than 3 days, people were less likely to vomit in the first day after chemotherapy (acute vomiting; odds ratio 0.4, 95% confidence interval 0.17 to 0.81; 3 trials, 301 people; moderate certainty by GRADE). There was no clear link with overall or delayed vomiting, or with how often or how badly people felt sick. A 2022 review of 23 trials found no difference overall in acute or delayed nausea or vomiting; only in trials with 1 g a day or less for more than 4 days was acute vomiting less common (odds ratio 0.30, 0.12 to 0.79). In these trials ginger was given with the usual anti-sickness medicines. The trials used powdered dried root in capsules (0.5 to 1.5 g a day for 3 to 5 days in several), but also a CO₂ extract, 6-gingerol capsules, an extract with 5% gingerols and ginger tea, which were not separated in the analysis.
findings.bottomLine: Added to usual anti-sickness medicines, ginger did not clearly reduce nausea or vomiting overall during chemotherapy. In smaller groups of trials with up to 1 g a day for several days, vomiting on the first day was less common. Trials mixed ginger root with concentrated extracts.
findings.label: Nausea during chemotherapy
findings.line: No clear change overall; less vomiting on day one in some groups of trials

findings.population: Young women with painful periods, mostly students in Iran, given crude dry ginger powder in capsules for the first days of one period
whyThisGrade: Few, small trials of poor methodological quality, with large differences between them
Five of the six trials in one review were in Iran, mostly following women for only one period
Side effects were rarely reported
In favour: every review found less pain than with a dummy pill, and all trials used plain dried ginger powder
findings.summary: A 2015 review pooled 4 trials comparing ginger with a dummy pill during the first 3 to 4 days of the period: the pain score (a visual analogue scale) was 1.85 lower (95% confidence interval 0.84 to 2.87), with 750 to 2,000 mg of ginger powder a day. A 2016 review of 6 trials found pain 1.55 cm lower on a 10 cm scale than with a dummy pill (0.68 to 2.43), and no difference from mefenamic acid, an anti-inflammatory painkiller (standardised mean difference 0, −0.40 to 0.41). All its trials used crude dry ginger powder; five were in Iran and one in India, mostly in students, usually over one period; the authors called the studies few, of poor quality and very different from each other. A 2024 review (12 trials pooled) found pain less intense (standardised mean difference −1.13, −1.59 to −0.68) and shorter (−0.29, −0.46 to −0.12) than with a dummy pill, and no difference from anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs) or exercise; safety was rarely reported.
findings.bottomLine: In small trials, mostly in Iranian students, dried ginger powder for the first days of a period lowered period pain compared with a dummy pill, by about 1.5 to 2 points on a 10-point scale, and did about as well as anti-inflammatory painkillers. The trials were few and of poor quality.
findings.label: Period pain
findings.line: About 1.5 to 2 points lower on a 10-point scale in small, poor-quality trials

findings.population: Adults with knee osteoarthritis given ground ginger in capsules (not extracts)
whyThisGrade: Only small trials of ground ginger: one blinded trial of 60 people and one open-label trial (people knew what they got) of 60
The blinded trial found no benefit; the open-label one found ginger added a little to a painkiller
The larger trials and the pooled benefit in reviews come from concentrated extracts, a different product (see What isn't known)
findings.summary: In a blinded trial, 60 people with knee osteoarthritis had 1 g of powdered ginger a day in a capsule or a dummy pill for 8 weeks: ginger did not improve knee pain, symptoms, daily activities, sport or quality of life, and caused no notable side effects. In an open-label trial, 60 people had diclofenac (a painkiller), 750 mg of ginger in capsules, or both, for 12 weeks: all three groups improved, the combination numerically most, with no significant difference in side effects. In 120 older people with knee osteoarthritis given daily capsules of 500 mg ginger powder or a dummy pill for 3 months, two inflammation signals in the blood (TNF-α and IL-1β) fell with ginger; the abstract reports only these blood signals, not pain.
findings.bottomLine: For knee osteoarthritis, trials of plain ground ginger are few and small: one blinded trial found no benefit over a dummy pill, and an open-label one found it added a little to a painkiller. The clearer benefits reported in reviews come from concentrated extracts.
findings.label: Knee arthritis pain
findings.line: No clear benefit from plain ground ginger in a few small trials

findings.outcome: Blood sugar and HbA1c in type 2 diabetes
findings.population: Adults with type 2 diabetes given 1,200 to 3,000 mg of ginger a day for 8 to 12 weeks, 10 of 13 trials in Iran
whyThisGrade: The newest review rated certainty low for fasting glucose and HbA1c: results differed a lot between trials
Mostly small, short trials from one country
A smaller 2024 review of 5 trials found no clear effect
Its authors judged the size of the changes of limited clinical importance
findings.summary: A 2026 review of 13 trials in type 2 diabetes found fasting blood glucose 16.27 mg/dL lower with ginger than with a dummy pill (95% confidence interval 6.80 to 25.75) and HbA1c 0.41 percentage points lower (0.20 to 0.63), with no change in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR). Results varied a lot between trials, the certainty was low for both, and the authors judged the size of the effects of limited clinical importance. Ten of the 13 trials were in Iran; they lasted 8 to 12 weeks with 1,200 to 3,000 mg of ginger a day. A 2022 review of 10 trials found similar falls (fasting glucose 18.81 mg/dL, HbA1c 0.57 points). A 2024 review that included only 5 trials, all of ginger powder in capsules at 1.2 to 2 g a day for 4 to 12 weeks, found no significant effect on fasting glucose or HbA1c.
findings.bottomLine: In short trials in type 2 diabetes, mostly in Iran, ginger went with slightly lower fasting blood sugar and HbA1c than a dummy pill. The certainty is low, one smaller review found no clear effect, and the authors called the changes of limited clinical importance.
findings.label: Blood sugar in type 2 diabetes
findings.line: Slightly lower fasting sugar and HbA1c in short trials, of limited clinical importance

findings.population: Adults in short ginger trials, many with type 2 diabetes or overweight
whyThisGrade: Triglycerides fell modestly in several reviews; LDL cholesterol did not clearly change
Certainty low for triglycerides and HDL, very low for LDL and total cholesterol in the newest review
Small, short trials with large differences between them
One review's LDL figures in its abstract don't agree with each other, so they are not used here
findings.summary: In the 2026 review of 13 trials in type 2 diabetes, triglycerides were 17.10 mg/dL lower with ginger than with a dummy pill (95% confidence interval 3.07 to 31.13) and HDL cholesterol 2.13 mg/dL higher (0.44 to 3.82), with low certainty; total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol did not change (very low certainty). A 2018 review of 12 trials (586 people) found triglycerides 17.59 mg/dL lower (5.87 to 29.32), no clear change in total cholesterol (−5.13, −11.05 to 0.78) or HDL; it also reported lower LDL, but the numbers in its abstract are inconsistent. A 2023 review found lower total cholesterol and triglycerides (standardised mean differences −0.44 and −0.61) and no clear change in HDL or LDL. A 2022 review of 10 trials in type 2 diabetes found no significant change in any blood fat.
findings.bottomLine: In short trials, ginger went with slightly lower triglycerides in several reviews, but LDL cholesterol did not clearly change and one review in diabetes found no change in any blood fat. Certainty is low.
findings.label: Cholesterol and triglycerides
findings.line: Small and inconsistent: triglycerides a little lower in several reviews, LDL unchanged

findings.population: Adults in short ginger supplement trials, including people with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure or obesity
whyThisGrade: The newest review rated certainty low (results differed between trials)
Trials were short; the fall in diastolic pressure was less robust
In type 2 diabetes alone the fall in systolic pressure was small (1.62 mmHg)
findings.summary: A 2026 review of 12 trials found systolic blood pressure 5.03 mmHg lower with ginger than without (95% confidence interval 1.57 to 8.49) and diastolic 2.03 mmHg lower (0.15 to 3.90), with low certainty by GRADE because results differed between trials. The falls were seen mainly in trials of people with raised blood pressure or obesity and with 2,000 mg a day or more; the authors note the trials were short. A 2019 review of 6 trials (345 people) found systolic pressure 6.36 mmHg lower (1.46 to 11.27) and diastolic 2.12 mmHg lower (0.31 to 3.92). In the 2026 review of trials in type 2 diabetes, systolic pressure was 1.62 mmHg lower (0.24 to 3.01; moderate certainty) and diastolic pressure did not change.
findings.bottomLine: In short trials, ginger supplements went with blood pressure a few mmHg lower than without, mostly in people with raised blood pressure or obesity. Certainty is low, and in type 2 diabetes the fall was small.
findings.label: Blood pressure
findings.line: A few mmHg lower in short trials, mostly in people with raised blood pressure or obesity

findings.outcome: Inflammation in the blood (CRP and other signals)
findings.population: Adults in ginger supplement trials, mostly people with a health condition
whyThisGrade: Very large differences between trials
CRP is a blood signal, not an illness: no trial showed fewer illnesses
The effect was seen mainly in people with health conditions
Reviews don't separate ground ginger from extracts
findings.summary: A 2025 review of 29 randomised trials found CRP 0.86 mg/L lower with ginger (95% confidence interval 0.62 to 1.10), with lower TNF-α and IL-6 (two other inflammation signals) and better measures of antioxidant status; the authors say the effect was clearest in people with health conditions and that the large differences between trials call for caution. A 2016 review of 9 studies found CRP 0.84 mg/L lower (0.31 to 1.38). A 2020 review of 16 trials (1,010 people) found lower CRP, high-sensitivity CRP and TNF-α, but no clear change in IL-6.
findings.bottomLine: In ginger supplement trials, CRP, a blood marker of inflammation, was a little lower (by under 1 mg/L) than without ginger, mostly in people with health conditions. Trials differed widely, and lower CRP is not the same as less illness.
findings.label: Inflammation (CRP)
findings.line: A little lower, by under 1 mg/L, in supplement trials that differed widely

whoShouldBeCareful.note: Ginger is among the most studied remedies for nausea in early pregnancy, and a cohort of 68,522 Norwegian women found no higher risk of birth defects, stillbirth or preterm birth in the 1,020 who used it. But the trials were small and short, and in one review miscarriage was not clearly more common with ginger, with a very wide uncertainty range (risk ratio 3.14, 0.65 to 15.11). A 2012 review argued that evidence of effect is not the same as proof of safety. Talk to your midwife or doctor before using ginger in capsules or other concentrated forms while pregnant, and about any severe or lasting vomiting.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Blood thinners (anticoagulants such as warfarin, or medicines against platelets)
whoShouldBeCareful.note: Ginger is often said to raise bleeding risk, but the evidence is weak and mixed. In a review of 8 trials, 4 found ginger lowered platelet clumping and 4 found no effect. In 12 healthy men, a ginger product for about 2 weeks did not change warfarin's effect on clotting (INR). In heart patients, 4 g of ginger powder a day for 3 months did not change platelet clumping, but a single 10 g amount did. One case report describes a 76-year-old woman on phenprocoumon whose INR rose to 10, with nosebleeds, weeks after she began ginger products. If you use a blood thinner, talk to your doctor before using ginger in capsules or other concentrated forms.

In trials in type 2 diabetes, ginger went with slightly lower fasting blood sugar and HbA1c (low certainty). No study found for this page looked at low blood sugar when ginger is added to medicines that lower blood sugar, so whether that happens isn't known. If you use such medicines, talk to your doctor before using ginger supplements.

cautions: Side effects in the trials were mostly mild and stomach-related. In the pregnancy review, heartburn and drowsiness were not more common with ginger; the 2006 surgery review reported only abdominal discomfort. In a trial of a concentrated extract (EV.EXT 77) for knee pain, stomach and gut side effects were more common with the extract (59 people against 21), mostly mild.

Ginger supplements differ a lot: in nine ginger root supplements analysed in 2007, the amount of 6-gingerol varied with a coefficient of variation of 115%, and ginger teas and drinks also varied widely.
In the chemotherapy trials, ginger was given alongside the usual anti-sickness medicines, not instead of them.
The pregnancy trials were in nausea and vomiting of early pregnancy. The Cochrane review left out hyperemesis gravidarum (severe, lasting vomiting in pregnancy), which needs a doctor or midwife.
unknowns: Knee osteoarthritis and extracts: a 2015 review of 5 trials (593 people) found modestly less pain (standardised mean difference −0.30, −0.50 to −0.09) and disability with ginger, and rated the evidence moderate, but the ginger trials in its reference list all describe a ginger extract in their titles, for example EV.EXT 77, a concentrated extract of ginger and galangal (261 people, 2001). People given ginger in that review were more than twice as likely to stop because of side effects (risk ratio 2.33, 1.04 to 5.22). Whether eating ginger does the same is not known.

How ginger might ease nausea is not settled. In 24 healthy people, 1,200 mg of ginger in capsules made the stomach empty faster; in cells, ginger extracts, 6-gingerol and 6-shogaol blocked serotonin 5-HT3 receptors, the target of some anti-sickness medicines. These are proposed explanations, not proof.
Whether fresh ginger, dried ginger, tea or cooked ginger differ in effect hasn't been tested head to head: most trials used ground ginger in capsules, and the chemistry differs between forms.
No trial has looked at long-term outcomes such as heart attacks, strokes or diabetes complications; the blood sugar, blood fat, blood pressure and CRP trials lasted weeks to a few months.
Most metabolic and period pain trials came from Iran, often small and with different amounts, so how far the results apply elsewhere is uncertain.
Ginger contains many compounds the food table doesn't measure (nutritional dark matter), and the trials can't say which of them, alone or together, explain any effect.
